message:
feat(update): the manifest is the container, and all three runtimes read it

A release is several files. The obvious way to ship several files is an archive;
this does not. The manifest lists each one -- name, size, SHA-256, URL -- and
the updater fetches and verifies them individually. One signature covers the
whole document, so a name cannot be paired with a different hash and a hash
cannot be paired with a different URL.

What skipping the archive buys is narrower than it first sounds, and worth
stating precisely: there is no compression or extraction code, so nothing there
can be got wrong. The attack surface does not disappear. The names and URLs in
this document still become filesystem paths and network requests, which is
exactly why both are checked before a verified manifest exists.

releaseId exists because of a specific failure. Fetching each file against
whatever "latest" says at the moment it is fetched lets a release change
underneath an update in progress, and the result is an install that is half one
build and half another. Every file staged for one attempt carries the same
identity.

The list has limits -- at most 64 artifacts, 512 MB each, 2 GB in total, with
the running sum checked so it cannot overflow past the ceiling on its way there.
A signed manifest is still one somebody could have made a mistake in. URLs must
be https and carry no credentials, enforced where the manifest is READ rather
than only where it is fetched, so a caller downloading some other way cannot
sidestep it.

All three runtimes moved together, because a schema only one of them
understands is not a contract. The shared vectors now carry three artifacts of
different sizes and contents, one of them GNLinkSetup.exe, and their bodies
ship alongside so a test can stage files whose hashes are the ones the manifest
claims. C++, JavaScript and Kotlin each verify that one signature.

Removing schema 1's handlers turned up a bug worth noting: its single-artifact
"artifact=" case ran first, so schema 2 lines never reached their branch. The
test caught it.

One transitional bridge, marked as such. The effects layer still stages a single
file, so a release containing exactly one artifact has its identity mirrored
into the legacy fields that layer reads. It deliberately does not fire for a
multi-artifact release -- nothing should quietly update using only the first of
several files.

Still missing, and not to be described otherwise: staging a whole release as one
snapshot, and the regressions that use real distinct files. The effects suite
copies one blob to several names, which verifies part of the OS path and is not
evidence that a multi-file update works.

qwinsta: console active, rdp-tcp listening. C++ 588 across eight suites, JS 54
plus the directory suite green, Kotlin 11 tests.
